part.distant.title: Distant opposition
part.distant.summary: After your move, leave an odd number of squares between the kings: the opposition is yours. The king goes ahead with it; the pawn advances later.
part.lateral.title: Lateral opposition
part.lateral.summary: On the same rank the count is the same: an odd number of squares between the kings, after your move, leaves the opposition with you.
part.capablanca.title: Capablanca's example
part.capablanca.summary: The side to move leaves an odd number of squares between the kings; if the other king changes file, wait and take the opposition back before moving up.
part.edge.title: Lateral approach
part.edge.summary: Going straight for the pawn can hand over the opposition. Step away: the other king cannot use the squares your pawns watch.
ex.e09: Play White and find the best move. Your king starts in the corner, far from the d2-pawn: bring it over with the distant opposition.
ex.e09.hint: First take your king to the black king's file, leaving an odd number of squares between them. Then, after each of his moves, keep the count.
ex.e09.solution:
1.Kg2! takes distant opposition on the g-file, with five squares between the kings. After 1...Kf7, 2.Kf3! maintains opposition on the f-file, now with three intervening squares. The exercise ends here: you have prepared the approach and preserved the win.

A continuation using the technique studied shows how to reduce the distance: 2...Ke6 3.Ke4 Kd6 4.Kd4. The kings reach direct opposition, on the pawn's file and in front of it. If White started with the pawn or with another king move, Black would draw.

These do not work either:

At move 1: The king is still in the corner: advancing the pawn before bringing the king out lets the defender occupy the centre. If White played 1.d3?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d3 Kf7 2.d4 Ke6. If White played 1.d4?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d4 Kf7 2.d5 Kf6.

At move 2: The approach must shorten the distance; staying back on the second rank lets the black king establish its defence. If White played 2.Kf2?, Black would reply 2...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf2 Ke6 3.d3 Kd5.
ex.e11: Play Black and find the best move. The white pawn is on c3 and the white king on e3. Your king must stop the white king from reaching the pawn's key squares: b5, c5 and d5.
ex.e11.hint: Take your king to the white king's file and leave an odd number of squares between them. When he changes file, do the same.
ex.e11.solution:
1...Ke7! Kings on e3 and e7, three squares between them, White to move: the distant opposition is yours. After 2.Kd3, 2...Kd7!, again with three squares between; after 3.Kc4, 3...Kc6!, now with a single square. The white king never reaches the c3-pawn's key squares, b5, c5 and d5. Any other first move lets the white king take the opposition, and at each step of the defence only one move holds.

These do not work either:

At move 1: Off the white king's file, or with an even number of squares between the kings, the white king takes the opposition. If Black played 1...Ke8?, White would reply 2.Kd4 and win. The line would be 1...Ke8 2.Kd4 Kd7 3.Kc5.

At move 2: After the change of file, the defence must follow the white king. If Black played 2...Kd6?, White would reply 3.Kd4 and win. The line would be 2...Kd6 3.Kd4 Kc7 4.Kc5.

At move 3: Stepping back or giving up the file opens a key square to the white king. If Black played 3...Kc7?, White would reply 4.Kb5 and win. The line would be 3...Kc7 4.Kb5 Kb7 5.Kc5. If Black played 3...Kc8?, White would reply 4.Kc5 and win. The line would be 3...Kc8 4.Kc5 Kb7 5.Kd6.
ex.e13: Play White and find the best move. The white pawn is on c3 and the kings are not yet on the same rank. Take your king to the black king's rank without letting him through.
ex.e13.hint: Look for the black king's rank, with an odd number of squares between the kings and Black to move.
ex.e13.solution:
1.Kd5! The kings stand on the same rank, with c5 between them and Black to move: the lateral opposition is yours. After 1...Kb6, 2.Kd6 repeats the idea on the next rank, again with one square between; 2.c4 and 2.Kd4 also win. The black king never gets through, and the white king escorts the pawn to promotion.

1.c4+? advances the pawn too soon: after 1...Kc6, 2.Ke4 Kc5, the black king plants itself in front of the pawn and it is a draw.
key.lesson: The white king takes the opposition from far away, with several squares between the kings, and closes the gap step by step until it reaches the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
key.capablanca: {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}}'s example: pawns facing each other, unable to advance, and the kings far apart. Whoever is to move takes the distant opposition and wins.
key.carlsenSo: {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, playing White, faced {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, playing Black, at {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017. Black was a pawn down and needed to prevent the white king from entering. The black king retreated to obtain distant opposition and followed its opponent from file to file; the game ended in a draw.
key.euweWhitaker: {{Max Euwe|max-euwe}}, playing White, faced {{Norman Whitaker|norman-whitaker}}, playing Black, in The Hague in 1928. The white king obtained distant opposition on the same rank as the black king, approaching the opposing pawn without allowing an equivalent race on the other wing. White won; observe how the kings’ relative positions help reach the target.
history:
Opposition is the contest between kings to force the opponent to give up space; it can begin at a distance or along a diagonal. The goal is to reach an important square, capture a pawn, or prevent an opposing entry. In his 1921 book Chess Fundamentals, {{José Raúl Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} explains the topic as an author through pawn-ending examples.

The technique also appears in games: at {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017, {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, playing Black, defended an ending a pawn down against {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, playing White. The black king followed the white king from a distance, and the game ended in a draw. Just a few pieces can conceal a precise contest for space and time.
practice: Now the real ending: king on h3, pawn on f3 and the black king on e6, eyeing the key squares e5, f5 and g5. Win the opposition on the diagonal, turn it into direct opposition and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.
ex.e09.r1: 1...Kf7. The black king leaves the g-file and heads for the centre, towards e6 and d5, in front of the d2-pawn. If the white king does not follow it with the distant opposition on the new file, Black takes it, and the pawn does not get through.
ex.e11.r1: 2.Kd3. The white king changes file, on its way to c4 and d4, from where it threatens to reach the c3-pawn's key squares: b5, c5 and d5. Ask yourself which square keeps your king in opposition after that change.
ex.e11.r2: 3.Kc4. The white king steps up to the fourth rank, one step from b5, c5 and d5. There is no room for the distant opposition now: it has to be direct.
ex.e13.r1: 1...Kb6. The black king steps up to b6 and escapes the opposition on the rank. Follow him onto his rank, again with one square between and Black to move.
title: Distant opposition
summary: Taking the opposition from afar, with an odd number of squares between the kings, to reach the key squares, protect the pawn and keep the enemy king out.
ex.e18: Play as White and find the best move. The b- and h-pawns face each other, unable to advance, and the black king is on the queenside. Find the route of your king to an enemy pawn.
ex.e18.hint: Take your king to the side the black king cannot reach in time: there, a pawn is left undefended.
ex.e18.solution: 1.Kg5! takes the king to the side where the black king is far away: the h5-pawn is left undefended. After 1...Kd5, 2.Kxh5! captures the pawn, and the h4-pawn is free to promote. 1.Kf5? and 1.Ke4? let the black king come back in time and draw.
ex.e18.r1: 1...Kd5. The black king goes to d5, towards the b4-pawn, trying to capture it before your king captures the one on h5.
ex.e19: Play as White and find the best move. The a-file pawns are locked and the black king is more active. Your king must reach the other side in time.
ex.e19.hint: It is a race: your king must go to meet the black king through the centre, without losing time, to get counterplay.
ex.e19.solution: 1.Kd7! starts the race against the black king. After 1...Kc5, 2.Ke6! heads for the centre; after 2...Kc4, 3.Ke5! and, after 3...Kc3, 4.Ke4! Your king arrives in time to defend and to attack the enemy pawn, and the draw is secured.
ex.e19.r1: 1...Kc5. The black king rushes to the centre and to the side of the a-file pawns.
ex.e19.r2: 2...Kc4. The black king drops another rank, threatening to enter on the queenside.
ex.e19.r3: 3...Kc3. The black king reaches c3 and threatens to go to b2 to attack the a2 pawn.
coach.allPartsDone: Now you know how to win the opposition and take your king to the key squares. Shall we go to the final test?
part.means.title: Choose the target
part.means.summary: Taking the opposition is not the goal: if your king can reach one of the pawn’s key squares directly, go there, even without the opposition.
key.means: The opposition is a means, not the goal: here taking it only draws. What wins is taking the king straight to the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
ex.e22: Play Black and find the best move. The pawns are locked, and your king must reach them before the white king comes back.
ex.e22.hint: Look for the side where the white king arrives too late, and see which squares the white pawns watch.
ex.e22.solution: 1...Kd7! takes the king to the queenside, away from the white king, where the white pawns watch neither b5 nor c4. After 2.Kg1, 2...Kc6! follows the same path: the king reaches b5, c4 and b3, captures the a3-pawn and clears the way for the a4-pawn. 1...Kf6? and 1...Ke6? bring the king closer to the white king, which arrives in time to defend the pawns, and it is a draw. 2...Kc7? also draws, because the king stays a rank behind.
ex.e22.r1: 2.Kg1. The white king moves to the first rank, far from the queenside pawns, and tries to come back through the centre.
ex.e21: Play White and find the best move. Both kings are far from the pawn, and the black king is already in the centre.
ex.e21.hint: The pawn's key squares are a4, b4 and c4. Ask yourself what matters more here: taking the opposition or getting close to those squares.
ex.e21.solution: 1.Kc2! The king heads for b3, next to all three key squares. After 1...Kd4, 2.Kb3! The black king cannot guard a4, b4 and c4 at the same time, and the white king gets into one of them. 1.Kd2? and 1.Ke2? move the king away from the pawn: the black king reaches the key squares first with 1...Kd4, and it is a draw. 1.b4? and 2.b3? also draw, because the pawn advances before the king. The opposition is a means; the goal is the key square.
ex.e21.r1: 1...Kd4. The black king approaches c4 and wants to reach the key squares before yours.
